evaluation.positioning_hook: After a blackout assault, a sorority freshman and her grocery-store best friend go undercover as frat bros to trap the predator, only to get seduced by the power, chaos, and lies of Greek life.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The hook is instantly legible and built around a high-recognition college setting, revenge energy, and broad comic set pieces. The content is sharp enough to travel, though the sexual-assault premise and explicit language narrow the buyer pool away from four-quadrant play.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands immediately in the opening assault sequence and then cleanly pivots into the undercover-frat engine. The cross-dressing / infiltration conceit is easy to explain in one breath and keeps the movie’s engine visible throughout.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Daisy and Maddy are distinct, funny, and built on a real friendship dynamic, while Tanner, Brad, Jake, Courtney, and Stephanie each have a usable comic function. The characters are strong enough to carry the feature, though the script leans more on premise and performance than on deep interiority.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script takes a familiar campus-comedy space and pushes it into a sharper, more confrontational lane by making the undercover game about assault, gaslighting, and fraternity power. The tonal confidence is real: it swings from broad raunch to social critique without losing its own voice.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The movie keeps resetting the objective with clear escalations: report the assault, infiltrate the frat, gather proof, survive the date party, then expose the whole system. The undercover beats, party reversals, and final Jungle sequence give it strong forward drive.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The central idea feels both fresh and immediately understandable: a campus assault story told through a frat-bro infiltration comedy. The gender-performance engine and the way the script weaponizes frat logic against itself give it a memorable, ownable twist.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Greek life is rendered as a social ecosystem with rituals, hierarchies, codes, and language that generate story: rush, pledging, Nationals, Tiki Bar, Jungle, Honor Council, Title IX. The sorority side is equally textured, which makes the campus feel like a functioning pressure cooker rather than a backdrop.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The voice is aggressively contemporary, profane, and joke-dense, but it also knows when to pivot into real discomfort and anger. The script has a recognizable register: raunchy, feminist, and socially pointed without becoming solemn.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Under the comedy, the script is really about complicity, denial, female friendship, and how institutions protect charismatic men. That depth is present in the Title IX scenes, Courtney’s turn, and the final campus fallout, though the movie mostly chooses propulsion over lingering psychological excavation.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Daisy/Maddy is a strong center, but the script also gives usable friction and chemistry to Daisy/Jake, Maddy/Stephanie, Daisy/Courtney, and the frat-bro ecosystem. Multiple pairings can generate scenes, which is a real asset for both casting and audience engagement.

lead_characters.name: Daisy
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 19, college freshman, sorority member, white.
lead_characters.hook: A golden-girl freshman who starts as the kind of campus social climber everyone underestimates, then gets forced into a crash course in shame, rage, and self-definition after a blackout assault. She’s funny, image-conscious, and deeply wounded, with a stubborn need for closure that keeps mutating into action.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a lead like Beanie Feldstein in Booksmart or Kathryn Newton in Abigail — a comic engine with real emotional bruising underneath. The role gives an actor the chance to play denial, humiliation, rage, and catharsis in the same movie, with a big physical transformation through the Derek disguise.

lead_characters.name: Maddy
lead_characters.demographics: Female, early 20s, college-age, working-class-coded, Daisy’s best friend, white.
lead_characters.hook: A grocery-store worker with a sharp mouth, a tomboy swagger, and a real outsider’s contempt for campus hierarchy. She’s the movie’s pressure valve and moral accelerant: funny, loyal, horny, and more clear-eyed than anyone else in the story.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Rachel Sennott in Shiva Baby or Ayo Edebiri in Bottoms a breakout lane — fast, specific, and scene-stealing without needing to be the formal protagonist. It offers a comic actor a chance to dominate scenes with timing, attitude, and a surprising emotional backbone.

lead_characters.name: Tanner
lead_characters.demographics: Male, mid-20s, Daisy’s friend’s older brother, local business owner, white.
lead_characters.hook: A reformed frat guy turned A/V dad-bro who becomes the movie’s tactical ally and absurdist coach. He’s goofy, unexpectedly useful, and emotionally lonely in a way that makes his masculinity feel both satirical and sincere.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of comic-supporting showcase that let Paul Rudd in Role Models or Adam Scott in Parks-adjacent material play competence with self-mockery. The role gives an actor a lot of buttoned-up comic authority, plus the chance to play the only adult in the room who still wants in on the chaos.

lead_characters.name: Brad
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 20s, fraternity brother, campus alpha, white.
lead_characters.hook: A charismatic predator who can switch from charming host to abusive manipulator without changing his smile. He’s not just a villain; he’s the movie’s embodiment of institutional gaslighting, social immunity, and frat-boy performance as power.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do the polished menace of Penn Badgley in You or the social ease of a classic campus antagonist while turning it dark. The showcase is in the pivot: charm, entitlement, panic, and collapse all in one performance.

lead_characters.name: Jake
lead_characters.hook: A sweet, awkward, emotionally porous freshman who keeps trying to be good and keeps getting pulled into the frat’s logic. He’s the movie’s most useful romantic decoy and one of its clearest examples of how the house trains boys to confuse passivity with decency.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives a young actor the same awkward-romantic territory that made Noah Centineo and Justice Smith pop in early breakout parts. The performance opportunity is in playing sincerity, confusion, and a late-blooming moral spine without losing the comedy.

lead_characters.name: Courtney
lead_characters.demographics: Female, early 20s, sorority member, Brad’s girlfriend, white.
lead_characters.hook: A former mean girl who starts as an obstacle and becomes one of the movie’s sharpest pivots toward solidarity. She’s wounded, image-aware, and more perceptive than she first appears, which makes her eventual alliance feel earned rather than tidy.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do the arc work of a Mean Girls-era antagonist who becomes emotionally legible by the end. It offers a strong turn from icy social power to wounded self-awareness and active resistance.

lead_characters.name: Stephanie
lead_characters.hook: An ethereal, hyper-competent sorority girl who initially reads as the straight-arrow prize and then becomes a surprisingly sharp witness to the campus ecosystem. She’s romantic, socially fluent, and more self-possessed than the boys realize.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the polished, deceptively light territory of a Rachel McAdams or Zoey Deutch campus part, with a late reveal of intelligence and agency. The showcase is in playing charm that can flip into judgment instantly.

lead_characters.name: Olivia
lead_characters.hook: Daisy’s quieter friend who starts as part of the social drift around the assault and later becomes part of the corrective force. She’s observant, dry, and useful in ensemble scenes without demanding the spotlight.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a solid supporting role for an actor who can play the grounded friend in a fast ensemble, similar to the best friend slots in Booksmart-style comedies. The appeal is in sharp reactions and the eventual shift from bystander to ally.

lead_characters.name: Kendall
lead_characters.hook: The more skeptical of Daisy’s friends, which gives her a useful edge in the opening fallout and later in the campus solidarity turn. She’s not the warmest person in the room, but she’s useful, funny, and believable as a peer who initially gets it wrong.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor play social defensiveness and then earn a turn toward conscience. It’s a compact but useful part for someone who can land sharp comic beats and then pivot into sincerity.

lead_characters.name: Harrison
lead_characters.hook: The house’s bureaucratic enforcer, always treating abuse like policy and humiliation like tradition. He’s a great comic institutional villain because he’s so committed to the rules that he never notices how monstrous they are.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor play dead-serious absurdity, like a campus version of a corporate functionary gone feral. The showcase is in playing authority as a joke that the character never realizes he’s in.

lead_characters.name: Theo
lead_characters.hook: A film-bro pledge with a cigarette habit and a fragile self-image, useful as both comic texture and a barometer for the frat’s moral rot. He’s vain, performative, and easy to manipulate, which makes him a good pressure-release character.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor a very specific comic lane: smug, fragile, and instantly legible. It’s a fun supporting part for someone who can make pretension funny without flattening the character.

lead_characters.name: Angelo
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 20s, fraternity pledge, NYC/Italian-American-coded, white.
lead_characters.hook: A loud, eager pledge whose need to belong makes him both funny and vulnerable. He’s one of the frat’s most humanized guys, which matters because he helps show how the house recruits insecurity as loyalty.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a juicy supporting part for an actor who can play big, eager, and emotionally transparent. The role gives you broad comedy plus a real turn in the final act when the house’s logic starts to crack.

casting_characteristics: Two central female roles require strong comedic chemistry
Multiple college-age male supporting roles with distinct frat archetypes
Lead requires physical comedy and emotional vulnerability
Several roles are age-flexible within early-20s range

notable_requirements: Frat house with basement, back rooms, bedroom, and party spaces
Sorority house with basement room and communal interiors
Campus exteriors, seminar room, grocery store, Title IX office, van interior, library, coffee shop

technical.vfx_details: No meaningful VFX beyond simple cleanup and title cards.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical vomit gag, fire gag on wig, branded-ass makeup/prosthetics, drug-test prop, party crowd control.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release; best suited to streaming or specialty theatrical with a mature-comedy audience.

budget.note: Contemporary and mostly interior, but the script needs multiple party nights, crowd scenes, a frat-house build, sorority-house spaces, and a significant night-shoot load.

casting.note: The lead needs to sell both wounded sincerity and broad undercover comedy, and the Daisy/Maddy pairing lives or dies on chemistry. Brad and Jake also need to be sharply differentiated without leaning on type alone.

development.note: The script’s engine is strong, but the tonal balance between assault-revenge, raunch comedy, and campus satire will be the main development conversation. The ending also asks the audience to track a lot of institutional fallout quickly.

comp_set.title: Booksmart
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the rapid-fire female friendship energy, campus specificity, and high-comedy confidence, even though this script is darker and more confrontational.

comp_set.title: Bottoms
comp_set.why_it_comps: The undercover, gender-performance, campus-comedy engine and anarchic tone are the clearest tonal neighbor, with a similar willingness to weaponize absurdity.

comp_set.title: The To Do List
comp_set.why_it_comps: The sexual coming-of-age, explicit joke density, and female-led campus setting make this a close packaging cousin on audience and tone.

comp_set.title: Neighbors
comp_set.why_it_comps: The frat-house warfare, party escalation, and broad campus-comedy mechanics live in the same commercial neighborhood.

comp_set.title: The Sex Lives of College Girls
comp_set.why_it_comps: The campus social ecosystem, female ensemble energy, and frank sexual politics align closely, even though this is a feature rather than a series.

audience_target.primary_audience: Gen Z and younger millennial viewers who want a raunchy, feminist campus comedy with real stakes and a revenge payoff.
audience_target.demographics: 18-34 skew, female-leaning but with male crossover from frat-comedy and college-party audiences; strongest with streaming-native viewers and college-educated audiences.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary college locations, a limited number of core sets, and no VFX-heavy sequences keep this in indie-feature territory, though the party nights and crowd work add some scope.

types_of_buyers: comedy directors looking for a breakout feature
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane of sharp, youth-skewing, female-led campus comedies with a social edge. The script’s combination of explicit humor, friendship chemistry, and institutional takedown gives it a clear buyer-facing identity.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature. The story resolves its central conflict cleanly, and no supporting character is built as a separate franchise anchor.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The undercover premise is instantly ownable.
strengths.what_it_means: This gives the project a clean marketing sentence and a visual hook that can sell in a thumbnail, trailer, or pitch meeting. Buyers looking for a female-led campus comedy with a sharper edge will immediately understand the engine.
strengths.evidence: Daisy and Maddy literally dress as guys, rush the frat, and use the disguise to infiltrate Brad’s world.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The Daisy-Maddy friendship carries the movie.
strengths.what_it_means: That relationship gives the film emotional traction beyond the joke machine and makes the comedy feel like it has a real heart. It also gives casting a clear two-hander chemistry test that can elevate the whole package.
strengths.evidence: Their secret handshake, ping-pong banter, and repeated “we work best as a pair” dynamic are the movie’s emotional spine.

strengths.what_it_means: The fraternity rituals, jargon, and social codes create a world that feels lived-in and story-generating, which is exactly what makes campus comedies rewatchable. That specificity also helps the script stand apart from generic college-party material.
strengths.evidence: Rush, pledging, Nationals, Jungle, the Tiki Bar, and the DIK house rules all function as recurring story mechanics.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The comedy is built on power reversal.
strengths.what_it_means: The script keeps turning frat logic back on itself, which makes the jokes feel structural rather than random. That’s a strong commercial trait because it creates repeatable set pieces and a satisfying revenge rhythm.
strengths.evidence: The girls learn the house’s language, win beer pong, weaponize “bro” behavior, and ultimately force Brad into a confession.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The final act broadens into campus accountability.
strengths.what_it_means: The movie doesn’t stop at one bad guy; it expands into a wider institutional takedown, which gives the ending more scale and relevance. That makes the project feel more current and more discussable for audiences and buyers alike.
strengths.evidence: The Tiki Bar drugging, Title IX fallout, campus police intervention, and postscript about other complaints all widen the scope.

whats_special.headline: This is a sharp, streaming-friendly campus comedy with a built-in hook: two young women go undercover in a frat to expose a predator, and the disguise engine keeps generating set pieces. The script pairs a marketable revenge premise with a real friendship core and enough Greek-life specificity to feel like a buyer can see the trailer immediately.

items.area: The assault premise narrows the buyer pool.
items.detail: The movie is built around sexual assault, drugging, and explicit frat abuse, which gives it urgency but also makes the content lane more sensitive than a standard college comedy. That’s a real positioning conversation for theatrical buyers and some streamers, even with the comic wrapper.

items.area: The final act stacks a lot of moving parts.
items.detail: The Jungle-party climax has undercover bait, a second infiltration, campus police, drug testing, a separate Jake/Tanner brawl, and the Brad confession all running at once. It plays with energy, but the density means the audience has to track a lot of simultaneous reversals in a short window.

items.area: The comedy leans hard on explicit language.
items.detail: The script’s voice is part of its appeal, but the volume of slurs, sexual references, and raunch jokes will be a factor in buyer conversations and marketing strategy. That’s not a creative flaw so much as a clear content identity that narrows the lane to buyers comfortable with hard-R comedy.

items.area: Brad’s confession arrives through a contrivance.
items.detail: The final bedroom scene depends on Daisy and Maddy forcing the confession through disguise, pressure, and a very specific lie chain. It’s satisfying as payoff, but it’s also the kind of engineered reveal a producer will clock as heavily plot-dependent.

items.area: The supporting ensemble is vivid but broad.
items.detail: Characters like Tanner, Jake, Courtney, Stephanie, Harrison, and Angelo are all useful and funny, but most are built as strong functions around the lead rather than deeply layered standalone roles. That helps the machine, but it also means the movie’s durability still rests heavily on Daisy and Maddy.

issues.headline: The biggest friction is not the premise — it’s the content lane and the density of the climax. This is a sharp, commercial campus comedy, but it’s also a hard-R assault-revenge movie with a lot of moving pieces in the final stretch, so buyers will want to know exactly how it’s being positioned.
